title: Athena, Glue & Lake Formation Data Lakes
summary: Query S3 with SQL, catalog and transform data with Glue, and govern it with Lake Formation.
tldr: **Athena** is serverless SQL on S3: no cluster, pay per data scanned. Cut cost and time by storing **columnar, compressed, partitioned** data (Parquet or ORC).
**AWS Glue** is serverless ETL plus the **Data Catalog** (the shared metastore for Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR). Crawlers discover schemas; **job bookmarks** process only new data.
**Lake Formation** adds central, database-style grants on the catalog: column-, row- and cell-level security through data filters and LF-Tags, instead of S3 bucket policies.
Need updates, deletes and ACID on S3? Use **Apache Iceberg** tables. Need fast dashboards for many users? **Amazon Quick Sight** with **SPICE**.

keyFacts.text: Athena bills by data scanned, so converting CSV to Parquet and partitioning by date often cuts cost and runtime by an order of magnitude.
Athena computes partition locations from table properties instead of calling the Glue catalog, which removes planning delay on tables with huge partition counts.
Glue remembers what each run already processed, so hourly jobs read only new S3 files. One setting, no custom tracking code.
Athena connectors (running on Lambda) query DynamoDB, RDS/Aurora, Redshift and others in place, joined with S3, with no ETL.
Quick Sight's in-memory engine. Import once on a schedule and dashboards stay fast without running a query per filter click.

traps: Moving data to a colder S3 class or turning on Transfer Acceleration does nothing for Athena scan cost; file format and partitioning do.
Running a crawler or `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` more often does not stop a Glue job from reprocessing old files; job bookmarks do.
Athena workgroups control query settings and cost limits, not row- or column-level access; that is Lake Formation.
Converting Parquet back to CSV makes queries slower and costlier; columnar formats are always the answer for analytics.
Redshift Spectrum needs a Redshift cluster or workgroup; for occasional queries with nothing in Redshift, Athena is cheaper.
